title: Sustainable and Equitable Services
editorial_note: Automated dialogue draft from the revised lesson. Review spoken wording and meaning before publishing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Today we're talking about Sustainable and Equitable Services. By the end, you'll know why this matters, how to use it, and what to notice in a real product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the problem we are trying to understand?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Good services consider who can access, understand, use, recover from, and leave the service—and who bears environmental, financial, time, and dignity costs. Equity means inspecting how a policy or channel distributes benefit and burden, not simply applying the same path to everyone.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why does that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Design multiple viable routes where circumstances differ, reduce unnecessary demands, and involve affected people in defining quality. Consider sustainability across the service system: travel, materials, energy, staff effort, repeat contacts, and preventable failure. Make trade-offs explicit rather than hiding them behind a single efficiency metric.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Examine who benefits, who pays, and whether the model endures
turns.text: What changes when we look at examine who benefits, who pays, and whether the model endures?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: An equitable service distributes access, burden, risk, and benefit fairly rather than giving everyone an identical route. A sustainable service can continue socially, operationally, financially, and environmentally without exhausting people or shifting hidden costs. These concerns belong in core service design, not a later ethics review.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The team models burden across actors. Self-service may reduce organisational cost while transferring data entry and coordination to patients. A 24-hour clinic promise may depend on coordinator overtime. Repeated notifications may increase infrastructure and attention cost without improving progress.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Options are evaluated against whole-life operation, maintenance, staffing, exclusion, and environmental effects.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Equity interventions are tested for unintended consequences and given owners, measures, and review dates. Assisted routes share the same service state and standards rather than becoming a neglected fallback. The final artifact is a distributional impact and sustainability register carried into prototyping and delivery.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: digital-only billing?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Removing paper may reduce cost and material use while excluding customers with low digital access and increasing support demand. A sustainable decision considers channel mix, accessibility, fraud, delivery reliability, and actual environmental lifecycle rather than one visible input.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at examine distribution across time?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Sustainability asks whether the service can continue delivering value within human, financial, technical, and environmental limits. Equity asks how benefits, burdens, delay, risk, and access are distributed. Analyse them together: a low-cost digital channel may exclude some people; a high-touch workaround may depend on invisible staff labour that cannot scale.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Map resources and externalities across the service lifecycle: devices, energy, travel, data, procurement, maintenance, staff capacity, customer time, and disposal or decommissioning. Avoid simplistic comparisons without system boundaries. The largest leverage may be policy, frequency, channel, or prevention rather than interface efficiency.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Test changes across groups and horizons. Who saves time now? Who supplies unpaid help? Does automation reduce repetitive work or concentrate more difficult cases? What happens when funding, volume, climate, or supplier conditions change?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Define minimum service standards, protected routes, capacity thresholds, and recovery. Monitor unequal abandonment, waiting, cost, staff burden, and environmental impact. A sustainable service does not achieve efficiency by making the least powerful people absorb its hidden costs.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Perform a distributional and whole-life review
turns.text: What changes when we look at perform a distributional and whole-life review?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Equity analysis examines mechanisms rather than using identity as a conclusion. Language, disability access, digital connection, geography, clinic capacity, work schedule, and helper availability can alter delay and recovery. Quantitative distribution identifies possible differences; lived and operational evidence explains them.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Unknown data is not treated as absence, and small high-consequence groups are not discarded for low statistical power.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Sustainability includes staff capacity, maintenance, supplier dependence, financial model, data lifecycle, energy and material use, and the ability to keep an alternative channel healthy. A concierge pilot that relies on expert overtime is not sustainable evidence.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A digital-only route may lower transaction cost while increasing devices, support, exclusion, and hidden family labour.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The team maintains an impact register with affected group or actor, mechanism, evidence, severity, mitigation, owner, measure, and review trigger. Trade-offs are made explicitly by accountable leaders and revisited after launch. Assisted routes share the same service records and standards so they do not become second-class fallbacks.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: paperless billing?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Removing paper may reduce material use and cost while excluding customers with limited digital access, increasing fraud exposure, and shifting printing elsewhere. A whole-life assessment compares channel mix, actual resource use, service reliability, and equitable access.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Do not frame equity as an edge case. A service’s “average” experience can conceal systematic barriers for people with less power, time, money, or access.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should we look at more closely?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Assess service value by how benefit and burden are distributed. Ask who can access, understand, complete, recover from, and leave the service; who absorbs time, travel, data, financial, environmental, or dignity costs; and whether one channel’s efficiency transfers work or harm elsewhere. Design multiple viable routes and include affected people in defining what quality means.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Failure modes to watch

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Digital-only efficiency: a fast default route excludes people without device, connectivity, language, payment, or confidence. Hidden burden shift: automation reduces one metric while moving work to staff, customers, or the environment. Equal treatment claim: identical paths ignore unequal resources and exposure to risk.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Unmeasured externality: sustainability or equity cost is outside the team’s success model.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A service makes digital-only booking fast for most customers. People without stable connectivity, language access, payment options, or device familiarity are pushed into slower and more expensive routes. Efficiency for one group has created exclusion for another.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: M11 has expanded UX from screens to service ecosystems, research, policy, measurement, and fairness. M12 moves into prototypes, critique, and evaluation—how teams learn before committing to costly change.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Choose a service. Identify one group for whom the default route is difficult, one burden shifted to staff or the environment, and one alternative service route.
